decks.title: Wrapper Classes, Autoboxing and Unboxing
goals: Distinguish primitive types from composite types and explain how a class creates a new type
Name the wrapper class of each of the eight primitive types
Define autoboxing and unboxing and identify them in code
Predict the result of statements that mix primitive values and wrapper objects

slides.heading: Wrapper classes
slides.body_md: Part 1: **primitive and composite types**, the eight **wrapper classes**, **autoboxing** and **unboxing**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: primitive and composite types, wrapper classes, autoboxing, unboxing, matching types and null
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome to the chapter on wrapper classes. In this first part we compare primitive and composite types, meet the eight wrapper classes of the package java dot lang, and learn how Java converts between a primitive value and a wrapper object by itself. These two conversions are called autoboxing and unboxing. We finish with the mistakes that beginners make most often.

slides.heading: Primitive and composite types
slides.body_md: A **primitive** type holds one simple value. A **composite** type is a **class**: it can hold several values together and has **methods**.

visual.alt: Table comparing primitive types and composite types: examples, what they hold, whether they have methods and who creates them

slides.narration: A primitive type, such as int, char or double, holds one simple value and has no methods. A composite type is a class. It can hold several values together, and it has methods. String is a composite type, and so is any class that you write yourself. The wrapper classes are also composite types, and each of them wraps one primitive value.

slides.heading: A class makes a new type

visual.caption: A class bundles several values into one new type.

slides.narration: A class lets a programmer create a new data type. The class Kite holds a colour and a length. An object of this type stores both values together, and the program prints red and thirty. A single int variable could not hold a word and a number at the same time. This is the idea of a composite type.

slides.heading: The eight wrapper classes
slides.body_md: Every primitive type has a **wrapper class** in the package **java.lang**, which Java imports automatically. A wrapper class wraps a primitive value in an object.

visual.alt: Table of the eight primitive types and their wrapper classes: byte Byte, short Short, int Integer, long Long, float Float, double Double, char Character, boolean Boolean, each with a declaration

slides.narration: Every primitive type has a wrapper class. Byte, Short, Integer, Long, Float, Double, Character and Boolean wrap byte, short, int, long, float, double, char and boolean. Six of them are the type name with a capital letter. Only int and char have longer names, Integer and Character. All eight belong to the package java dot lang, which Java imports by itself.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: choosing the wrapper

visual.alt: Table choosing a wrapper class for each value; the program prints 48 K true 99.5 4200000000
visual.caption: Printed together: `48 K true 99.5 4200000000`

slides.narration: Let us choose a wrapper for each value. The whole number forty eight goes into an Integer. The letter K goes into a Character. True goes into a Boolean. Ninety nine point five is a double, so it needs a Double. A long literal, such as four billion two hundred million, needs a Long. The program prints all five values on one line.

slides.heading: Quick check: primitive and wrapper
slides.body_md: Match each primitive type with its wrapper class.
slides.narration: Recall the eight wrapper classes. Remember that int and char have the longer names.

slides.heading: Why an object helps
slides.body_md: An **object** can call methods; a **primitive** variable cannot. Wrapper classes also carry useful methods and constants.

rows: compile-time error: int cannot be dereferenced

visual.alt: Table showing that a call on an int variable is a compile-time error with the message int cannot be dereferenced, while the same call on an Integer object prints 5
visual.caption: Only an object can call a method.

slides.narration: A wrapper object can call methods, but a primitive variable cannot. In the table, calling to string on an int variable gives a compile time error, int cannot be dereferenced. The same call on an Integer object works and gives the text five. Wrapper classes also carry useful methods and constants, which we use throughout this chapter.

slides.heading: Making a wrapper object
slides.body_md: The method **valueOf** returns a wrapper object. Constants such as `Integer.MAX_VALUE` give the limits. The constructors, such as `new Integer(25)`, are **deprecated since Java 9**: do not use them.

visual.alt: Table of wrapper objects and constants: valueOf of 25 gives 25; the largest int is 2147483647 and the smallest is -2147483648; the largest long is 9223372036854775807
visual.caption: The constants give the limits of each type.

slides.narration: A wrapper object can be made with the valueOf method, for example Integer dot valueOf of twenty five. The old constructors, such as new Integer, are deprecated since Java nine, so we do not use them. Each wrapper class also has constants for the limits of its type. The largest int is more than two billion. The easiest way to make a wrapper object is autoboxing, coming next.

slides.body_md: Decide whether the statement is true or false.
slides.narration: Count the primitive types of Java and the wrapper classes. Do the numbers agree?

slides.heading: Autoboxing
slides.body_md:
**Autoboxing** is the automatic conversion of a **primitive value into a wrapper object**.

```java
int a = 40;
Integer boxed = a;      // autoboxing
int back = boxed + 2;   // unboxing, then addition
System.out.println(boxed + " " + back);
```

visual.caption: Autoboxing puts the value into an object; unboxing takes it out.

slides.narration: Autoboxing is the automatic conversion of a primitive value into an object of its wrapper class. In the program, the int variable a is stored in the Integer variable boxed with no method call at all. Java creates the wrapper object for us. The picture shows the value forty inside an object. Boxing always goes from the primitive to the object.

slides.heading: Unboxing
slides.body_md: **Unboxing** is the automatic conversion of a **wrapper object into the primitive value** it holds. It happens in assignments, arithmetic and comparisons.

headers: Where the Integer boxed (40) is used

visual.alt: Table of unboxing in four places for an Integer holding 40: assignment to an int gives 40, addition of 2 gives 42, comparison with 30 gives true, multiplication by 1.5 gives 60.0
visual.caption: In each case the number is taken out of the object first.

slides.narration: Unboxing is the reverse. The primitive value is taken out of the wrapper object automatically. It happens when an Integer is assigned to an int variable, and when an Integer is used in arithmetic or in a comparison. With boxed holding forty, boxed plus two is forty two, boxed greater than thirty is true, and boxed times one point five is sixty point zero.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: tracing the conversions

visual.alt: Trace table of the card program: base is 25, card is 25 after boxing, card is 35 after the addition and paid is 70; the output is 35 70
visual.caption: Output: `35 70`

slides.narration: Trace the program line by line. The int twenty five is boxed into card. In card plus ten, the object is unboxed, ten is added, and the result thirty five is boxed again into card. Then card times two unboxes it once more, and paid becomes seventy. The program prints thirty five and seventy.

slides.heading: Boxing inside expressions
slides.body_md: Statements such as `total = total + 5;` and `total++;` on an Integer **unbox, calculate and box again**. They look like ordinary arithmetic.

visual.alt: Table of boxing inside statements: total is 10, then 15, then 16; half is 8.0
visual.caption: The statements look like ordinary arithmetic, but wrapper objects are converted each time.

slides.narration: Boxing and unboxing can happen several times in one statement. In total equals total plus five, the Integer is unboxed, five is added, and the sum is boxed back into total. Even total plus plus works the same way. The code does not look different, but behind the scenes each step converts between the primitive value and the object.

slides.heading: Quick check: unboxing
slides.body_md: Fill in the blank.
slides.narration: Remember the name of the process that takes the primitive value out of a wrapper object.

slides.heading: Boxing needs the matching type
slides.body_md: A primitive is boxed **only into the wrapper of its own type**. The literal `5` is an int, so it fits an `Integer` but not a `Double` or a `Long`.

rows: error: incompatible types: int cannot be converted to Double
error: incompatible types: int cannot be converted to Long
error: incompatible types: long cannot be converted to Integer

visual.alt: Table of boxing declarations: Integer a = 5, Long b = 5L and Double c = 5.0 compile; Double c = 5 gives incompatible types: int cannot be converted to Double; Long d = 5 gives incompatible types: int cannot be converted to Long; Integer e = 5L gives incompatible types: long cannot be converted to Integer
visual.caption: The literal must have the type of the wrapper.

slides.narration: Autoboxing works only with the wrapper of the same type. The literal five is an int, so it can go into an Integer. A Double needs a double literal such as five point zero, and a Long needs a literal ending in the letter L. Writing Double c equals five makes javac report that int cannot be converted to Double. Always match the literal with the wrapper.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: finding the conversions

rows: unboxing: the Integer is used as an int

visual.alt: Table naming the conversion in each line of the fee program: line 1 none, line 2 autoboxing, line 3 unboxing; the value of left is 380
visual.caption: Output: `380`

slides.narration: Let us find the conversions in three lines. The first line stores an int in a primitive variable, so nothing is converted. In the second line the int fee goes into an Integer variable, which is autoboxing. In the third line the Integer is used in a subtraction and the result is stored in an int, which is unboxing. The value of left is three hundred eighty.

slides.heading: null and unboxing
slides.body_md: A wrapper variable can hold **null**, which means no object. **Unboxing null** throws a **NullPointerException** at run time; the compiler cannot detect it.

rows: A wrapper data member that was never assigned
run-time error: java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "java.lang.Double.doubleValue()" because "this.due" is null
no error: the compiler cannot know the value

visual.alt: Table of unboxing null: a wrapper data member never assigned holds null; unboxing it stops the program at run time with java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "java.lang.Double.doubleValue()" because "this.due" is null; the compiler reports no error

slides.narration: A wrapper variable can hold null, which means that there is no object. Unboxing a null reference fails at run time with a null pointer exception, because there is no value inside. In the Ledger program, the data member due was never assigned, so the statement that unboxes it stops the program. The compiler cannot catch this, so it is a run time error.

slides.heading: Quick check: matching types
slides.body_md: Choose the correct option for the assertion and the reason.
slides.narration: Think about the type of the literal and the wrapper class that it can be boxed into.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: a primitive holds one value; a class bundles values and methods
eight, in java.lang: Byte, Short, Integer, Long, Float, Double, Character, Boolean
primitive value to wrapper object, automatically
wrapper object to primitive value, automatically
an int boxes only into an Integer, a double only into a Double
unboxing null throws NullPointerException at run time

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: primitive and composite types, the eight wrapper classes, autoboxing, unboxing, matching types and null

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. A primitive holds one value, and a class is a composite type. The eight wrapper classes live in java dot lang. Autoboxing converts a primitive to a wrapper object, and unboxing converts it back, both automatically. A primitive is boxed only into the wrapper of its own type. Unboxing a null reference stops the program with a null pointer exception.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Learn the pairs: `int` with `Integer` and `char` with `Character`; the other six add a capital letter.
To find boxing, look for a primitive stored in a wrapper variable; for unboxing, a wrapper used as a number.
A literal must match the wrapper: `Double d = 5;` is an error, `Double d = 5.0;` is correct.
Do not write `new Integer(5)`: it is deprecated. Use autoboxing or `valueOf`.
An error question needs the kind of error (compile-time or run-time) and the reason.
slides.narration: Some exam tips. Learn the pairs: int goes with Integer and char goes with Character, and the other six add a capital letter. To find boxing, look for a primitive stored in a wrapper variable. For unboxing, look for a wrapper used as a number. A literal must match the wrapper. Do not use the deprecated constructors. In error questions, state the kind of error and the reason.

decks.title: Parse Methods and Character Methods
goals: Convert numeric Strings to numbers with parseInt, parseLong, parseFloat and parseDouble and predict the results
Predict the output of Character methods that test and convert characters
Write programs that classify the characters of a String

slides.heading: Parse and Character methods
slides.body_md: Part 2: **parseInt**, **parseLong**, **parseFloat** and **parseDouble**; the methods of the **Character** class; classifying the characters of a String.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: why parse, the four parse methods, NumberFormatException, valueOf and toString, Character tests, case conversion and classifying a String
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome to the second part. We learn how to turn a numeric string into a number with parseInt, parseLong, parseFloat and parseDouble, and what happens when the text is not a valid number. Then we study the Character class: methods that test a character and methods that change its case. We finish by classifying every character of a string with a loop.

slides.heading: Why convert text into numbers?
slides.body_md: Text typed by a user is a **String**. The operator `+` **joins** Strings; it does not add them. Convert with a **parse** method first.

rows: compile-time error: bad operand types for binary operator '*'

visual.alt: Table showing that plus joins two Strings and gives 205, that parseInt makes plus add the numbers to give 25, and that multiplying Strings is a compile-time error: bad operand types for binary operator '*'
visual.caption: Convert a String with a parse method before doing arithmetic.

slides.narration: Text typed by a user arrives as a String. The plus operator joins two Strings, so twenty plus five gives two hundred and five, as text. After converting each String with parseInt, the same plus adds the numbers and gives twenty five. A String cannot be multiplied at all, and javac reports a bad operand error. So we convert first.

slides.heading: The four parse methods

visual.alt: Table of the four parse methods with the type returned and the value for the text 205: Integer.parseInt returns int, value 205; Long.parseLong returns long, value 205; Float.parseFloat returns float, value 205.0; Double.parseDouble returns double, value 205.0
visual.caption: Each parse method takes a String and is called with the class name.

slides.narration: There is one parse method for each numeric type. parseInt returns an int, parseLong returns a long, parseFloat returns a float, and parseDouble returns a double. Each takes a String as its argument. They are static methods, so we call them with the class name, for example Integer dot parseInt. Use parseLong when the number is too big for an int.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: adding typed amounts

visual.alt: Table of two runs of the amount program: input 120.50 79.50 gives 200.0 and input 10 15 gives 25.0
visual.caption: parseDouble gives a double, so the sum always has a decimal point.

slides.narration: Let us add two amounts typed as text. The program reads two words and converts each with parseDouble. For one hundred twenty point five zero and seventy nine point five zero, the sum is two hundred point zero. For ten and fifteen, the sum is twenty five point zero. A double always shows at least one digit after the point.

slides.heading: Quick check: the steps
slides.body_md: Arrange the steps of the program in order.
slides.narration: Think about what must happen before two typed words can be added.

slides.heading: Signs, decimals and doubles
slides.body_md: A leading `+` or `-` and leading zeros are accepted. `parseInt` **rejects a decimal point**. `parseDouble` accepts whole numbers and gives a double. Big numbers need `parseLong`.

visual.alt: Table of results: Integer.parseInt("+7") gives 7; Integer.parseInt("-15") gives -15; Integer.parseInt("007") gives 7; Integer.parseInt("12.5") gives java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "12.5"; Double.parseDouble("3") gives 3.0; Long.parseLong("4000000000") gives 4000000000
visual.caption: A sign and leading zeros are accepted; a decimal point is not accepted by parseInt.

slides.narration: Look at what the parse methods accept. A leading plus or minus sign is fine, so parseInt of plus seven gives seven. Leading zeros are accepted too. But parseInt rejects a decimal point. parseDouble accepts a whole number, and parseDouble of three gives three point zero. parseLong is needed for big numbers such as four billion.

slides.heading: NumberFormatException
slides.body_md: If the text is not a valid number, the parse method throws **NumberFormatException** and the program stops. A decimal point, a letter, an empty text and even a **space** make `parseInt` fail.

visual.alt: Table of texts that parseInt rejects, with the real messages: java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "12.5"; java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: " 42"; java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "42 "; java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "abc"; java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: ""
visual.caption: The message shows the text that failed. This is a run-time error.

slides.narration: When the text is not a valid number, the parse method throws a NumberFormatException, and the program stops. The message shows the exact text that failed. A decimal point, a letter, an empty string and even a space before or after the digits make parseInt fail. This is a run time error, not a compile time error.

slides.heading: Quick check: a failing conversion
slides.body_md: State the error that the program causes.
slides.narration: Look at the text given to parseInt. Is every character a digit?

slides.heading: Worked example 2: which texts convert?
slides.body_md: Test five texts with both `parseInt` and `parseDouble`. A cell shows the exception when the conversion fails.

visual.alt: Table of five texts converted with parseInt and parseDouble: 25: 25 and 25.0; 25.5: NumberFormatException and 25.5; -8: -8 and -8.0; 1,5: NumberFormatException and NumberFormatException; abc: NumberFormatException and NumberFormatException
visual.caption: A failure throws NumberFormatException and stops the program.

slides.narration: Let us test five texts with both methods. The text twenty five works with both. Twenty five point five works only with parseDouble. Minus eight works with both. A comma between digits and a word fail with both. Notice that a failure stops the program, so in real programs the input must be valid.

slides.heading: parseInt, valueOf and toString
slides.body_md: **parseInt** returns a primitive **int**; **valueOf** returns an **Integer** object; **toString** turns a number into a **String**.

visual.alt: Table of the type returned: parseInt gives an int, valueOf gives an Integer object, toString gives a String, parseDouble gives a double
visual.caption: parse gives a primitive, valueOf gives an object, toString gives text.

slides.narration: Three related methods differ in what they return. parseInt returns a primitive int. valueOf returns a wrapper object, an Integer, and it can also take a String. toString goes the other way and returns a String made from a number. When they are printed, the first two look the same, but their types are different.

slides.heading: Compile-time errors with parse methods
slides.body_md: Some mistakes are found by the compiler: a **wrong argument type**, a **lossy conversion** and a **method that does not exist**.

rows: incompatible types: int cannot be converted to String
incompatible types: possible lossy conversion from double to int

visual.alt: Table of compile-time errors with parse methods: incompatible types: int cannot be converted to String; incompatible types: possible lossy conversion from double to int; cannot find symbol
visual.caption: These are caught by the compiler; NumberFormatException is not.

slides.narration: Some mistakes are caught by the compiler. Passing a number instead of a String gives incompatible types. Storing the double from parseDouble in an int variable gives a lossy conversion error. And Integer has no method called parseLong, so javac says cannot find symbol. Compare these with the run time NumberFormatException, which comes from the text itself.

slides.body_md: Choose the correct statement.
slides.narration: Remember which of the two methods returns a primitive and which returns an object.

slides.heading: Character methods that test
slides.body_md: Each method takes one **char** and returns **true** or **false**. Note that `isLetterOrDigit` is true for letters **and** digits.

visual.alt: Table of the true or false results of six Character methods for the characters a, K, 5, space and hash: isLetter: true, true, false, false, false; isDigit: false, false, true, false, false; isLetterOrDigit: true, true, true, false, false; isLowerCase: true, false, false, false, false; isUpperCase: false, true, false, false, false; isWhitespace: false, false, false, true, false
visual.caption: Each method takes one char and returns a boolean.

slides.narration: The Character class has methods that test one character and return true or false: isLetter, isDigit, isLetterOrDigit, isLowerCase, isUpperCase and isWhitespace. In the table, the letter a is a letter and lower case, the five is a digit, the space is white space, and the hash sign is none of these. Remember that isLetterOrDigit is true for both letters and digits.

slides.heading: Methods that change case
slides.body_md: **toUpperCase** and **toLowerCase** take a char and **return a char**. They do not change the variable: store or print the result.

visual.alt: Table of case conversion: toUpperCase of g gives G; toLowerCase of M gives m; toUpperCase of 4 gives 4; toLowerCase of # gives #
visual.caption: Digits and symbols have no case and come back unchanged.

slides.narration: toUpperCase and toLowerCase take a char and return a char. The letter g becomes capital G, and capital M becomes small m. A digit or a symbol has no case, so it comes back unchanged. These methods do not change the original variable. They return a new value, which must be stored or printed.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a char in arithmetic
slides.body_md: Trace `Character.toUpperCase('d')` used alone, with `+ 1`, and with a cast to `char`.

visual.alt: Table of a char in arithmetic: toUpperCase of d displays D; adding 1 gives the int 69; a cast to char gives E
visual.caption: In arithmetic a char is replaced by its integer code.

slides.narration: Now see what happens when the returned char is used in arithmetic. toUpperCase of d returns capital D, which prints as a letter. But adding one replaces D by its integer code, sixty eight, so the result is sixty nine, a number. To print the next letter, cast the sum to char. The output is capital E.

slides.body_md: Write the exact output.
slides.narration: Convert each character, and notice what happens to the digit and to the last line, where two chars are added.

slides.heading: Classifying the characters of a String

nodes.label: After the loop: display the counters

visual.alt: Flow of a loop that classifies the characters of a String: start with i equal to 0, test i less than length, pick the character with charAt, test it and update a counter, increase i, and display the counters after the loop
visual.caption: The pattern behind most String programs of this chapter.

slides.narration: To classify all the characters of a String, use a loop. The index i goes from zero up to length minus one. In each pass, charAt of i picks one character, and Character methods decide which counter to increase. The counters are displayed after the loop. This pattern is the basis of password checkers, word counters and case changers.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: counting letters, digits and others

visual.alt: Trace table of the loop for the text Bay 9A#: the final counts of letters, digits and other characters are 4 1 2
visual.caption: Output: `4 1 2`

slides.narration: Let us trace the loop for the text Bay, space, nine, A, hash. The characters B, a and y are letters. The space is counted as other. The digit nine increases the digit counter. Then A is the fourth letter and the hash sign is the second other character. The final counts are four letters, one digit and two other characters.

slides.heading: Typical programs
slides.body_md: The same pattern, with different tests, gives many programs. A **PIN validator** also converts the text with `parseInt` after checking every character.

sections.body_md:
**Autoboxing** is the automatic conversion of a primitive value into an object of its wrapper class. **Unboxing** is the automatic conversion of a wrapper object into the primitive value it holds. Unboxing happens in assignments to primitive variables, in arithmetic and in comparisons.

```java
int a = 40;
Integer boxed = a;      // autoboxing
int back = boxed + 2;   // unboxing, then addition
System.out.println(boxed + " " + back);
```

Output: `40 42`.

Boxing inside expressions: `total = total + 5;` on an Integer unboxes, adds and boxes again.

**Common mistakes**
- Writing `Double d = 5;` (an int is boxed only into an Integer) or `Long n = 5;`.

- Output questions: each line in the exact order and format; a char in arithmetic shows a number.
- Error questions: the kind of error (compile-time or run-time), the line or exception and the reason.
- Programs (15 marks): structure and input, the loop or conversion, the Character or parse methods used correctly, output with messages, variable description or comments.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A primitive variable holds a single simple value, while a composite type (a class) can bundle several values and methods together. A class is a composite type: for example a class Kite with the data members String colour and int length bundles a String and an int, and one Kite object prints `red 30`.
